column5: no prophetic word allowed to fall to the ground
column6: The commentary makes “you will not forget” the result of God-held recitation and contrasts it with a word dropped like worthless debris. Samuel grows with YHWH, who lets none of his words fall to the ground; this prophetic formula gives a close Hebrew Bible image for divinely sustained speech that does not fall away.

column5: commandments placed upon the heart
column6: The commentary has the given word gathered within the recipient before it is voiced. Deuteronomy places these words upon Israel's heart, an early covenant formulation of interior retention that stands behind later oral teaching.

column5: words repeatedly taught and spoken in daily life
column6: The commentary moves from retained recitation to passing the word outwardly. Deuteronomy requires parents to teach the words diligently and speak of them through the ordinary rhythms of day and night, making memory a recurrent oral practice.

column5: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
column6: The commentary's ق ر ء material treats reading as voiced words received by listeners. At the pilgrimage assembly Moses is commanded to read the Torah in all Israel's hearing so that they hear, learn, and fear; the Hebrew קרא is the cognate in a public instructional setting.

column5: God's Torah kept in the mouth as a memorial
column6: The commentary joins unforgotten recitation to memory of the divine giver. Exodus calls the festival sign a memorial so that YHWH's Torah may be in Israel's mouth, making oral retention a ritualized response to deliverance.

column5: Moses writes all the words of YHWH
column6: The commentary brings oral recitation beside the earlier pages of Moses. Before the public reading of the covenant book, Moses writes all YHWH's words; this supplies the written half of the oral-and-page sequence developed in the commentary.

column5: testimony bound up and teaching sealed among disciples
column6: The commentary describes a message whose path to the messenger is guarded and whose retention is secured by its giver. Isaiah orders the testimony bound and the teaching sealed among disciples, a compact image of protected instruction held within a defined receiving community.

column5: prophecy inscribed on tablet and book for future time
column6: The commentary's final pages carry words beyond the first recipient. Isaiah is told to write the message before the people on a tablet and in a book so it remains for a future day, a direct preservation scene for revelation meant to outlast its first utterance.

column5: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
column6: The commentary pairs gathering with a recited word that is not lost. Isaiah tells hearers to seek and read from YHWH's book, says none will be missing, and grounds the gathering in YHWH's mouth and Spirit; Hebrew קרא supplies the cognate reading verb within an unusually close no-omission context.

column5: divine words put in a mouth and protected by God's hand
column6: The commentary's addressee speaks a word he did not originate and is kept by the speaker who gave it. Isaiah says God has put words in the servant's mouth and covered him with the shadow of the divine hand, joining enabled speech to protection.

column5: a word shut up inside that cannot be held back
column6: The commentary's womb image gives the retained word a later outward release. Jeremiah tries not to mention or speak in God's name, but the word becomes a fire shut in his bones which he cannot contain; it offers a bodily image of inward revelation pressing toward proclamation.

column5: God's true word spoken faithfully over against straw
column6: The commentary puts its undropped word immediately after pasture becomes refuse. Jeremiah distinguishes a dreamer's report from one who has God's word and must speak it faithfully, then contrasts straw with wheat; it joins trustworthy utterance to the commentary's vegetation-and-chaff contrast.

column5: God's words found and eaten
column6: The commentary's language of gathering inside the recipient is not limited to intellectual recall. Jeremiah finds and eats God's words, which become joy and delight, a prophetic ingestion image that complements the scroll-eating scenes without merely repeating them.

column5: all divine words received in heart and heard with ears
column6: The commentary insists that the recipient follows a word first supplied by its teacher. Ezekiel is told to receive in his heart all the words God speaks and to hear them with his ears, explicitly joining inward reception and attentive listening before his mission.

column5: God opens the prophet's mouth when speaking to him
column6: The commentary reads the causative form as God making the addressee able to recite. After controlling Ezekiel's silence, God says that when he speaks with him he will open the prophet's mouth; the verse makes the possibility of prophetic utterance depend on divine initiative.

column5: vision written plainly so a reader can run with it
column6: The commentary holds recitation together with ordered pages and a message carried onward. Habakkuk is told to write the vision clearly on tablets so that its reader may run, a scene where a fixed written revelation enables its bearer to transmit or act on it.

column5: Torah read, then confessed and worshipped
column6: The commentary ends by joining reading to prayer and worship rather than treating it as bare sound. Nehemiah's community spends part of the day reading the Torah and another part confessing and worshipping, a liturgical realization of received words becoming devotion.

column5: God-written tablets given to Moses for teaching
column6: The commentary's “pages of Moses” are words received from God and then given onward. Jubilees has God promise Moses tablets of law and commandment that God has written so Moses may teach them, a Jewish retelling that makes both divine authorship and transmission explicit.

column5: the heard word held fast in a good heart and bearing fruit
column6: The commentary's word is retained in the recipient and subsequently released in beneficial reminder. In Luke's good-soil explanation, hearers hold the word fast in an honest heart and bear fruit with endurance, making fruitful outward consequence depend on inward retention.

column5: words received from the Father, given by Jesus, and received by disciples
column6: The commentary follows revelation from its source through a messenger to those addressed. Jesus says he gave disciples the words the Father gave him and that they received them; this is a three-stage Johannine account of sourced and accepted speech.

column5: the Father commands what Jesus must say and speak
column6: The commentary distinguishes the one who recites from the one who causes the recitation. Jesus says he has not spoken from himself because the Father who sent him commanded what he should say and speak, a closely related claim of divinely determined utterance.

column5: the Spirit speaks what it hears and guides into truth
column6: The commentary has the recipient follow the giver's recitation rather than create an independent message. Jesus describes the Spirit of truth as not speaking from itself but speaking what it hears while guiding disciples, a Christian messenger model of received speech.

column5: Spirit-filled believers speak God's word
column6: The commentary's “we will cause you to recite” attributes enabled proclamation to God. After prayer, the gathered believers are filled with the Holy Spirit and speak God's word with boldness, a communal narrative of divinely empowered speech.

column5: words taught by the Spirit rather than human wisdom
column6: The commentary frames the recipient's reading as teaching received from a transcendent source. Paul says that he and his colleagues speak in words taught by the Spirit rather than human wisdom, a Christian articulation of divinely instructed expression.

column5: gospel received through revelation rather than human teaching
column6: The commentary denies that the addressee independently produces the recitation. Paul says he neither received nor was taught his gospel by a human being but received it through revelation of Jesus Christ, a direct source-of-message parallel.

column5: God's word received as divine and active within believers
column6: The commentary says the given word is held within the recipient, not merely heard as an external sound. The Thessalonians receive the preached word as God's word rather than a human one, and Paul says it is at work within believers; this connects reception to inward efficacy.

column5: the implanted word received with meekness
column6: The commentary's pregnancy analogy presents the word as held within a body before outward consequence. James calls the saving word “implanted” and commands its reception, a concise Christian image of a word placed within and able to generate life.

column5: new birth through the living and enduring word
column6: The commentary pairs womb, retention, and release with the word's not being discarded. First Peter attributes new birth to the living and abiding word of God, a Christian use of birth imagery that makes the enduring word generative.

column5: Torah scroll placed beside the ark as a witness
column6: The commentary's old pages are preserved so their word is not lost. Moses orders the completed Torah scroll placed beside the ark as a witness; this is a material practice of keeping a received text available beyond immediate oral memory.

column5: a sealed book offered to one who says he cannot read it
column6: The commentary's promise is that God will enable the addressee to recite and will preserve the word, while it also reflects on hidden and manifest speech. Isaiah's vision becomes a sealed book that even a reader cannot read; the contrast makes divine enablement, rather than literacy alone, the issue.

column5: instruction written on the tablet of the heart
column6: The commentary joins pages to a word held in the recipient. Proverbs tells the pupil to bind the commands and write them on the tablet of the heart, a wisdom-text counterpart to inward inscription and memorized guidance.

column5: not forgetting God's works while keeping commandments
column6: The commentary uses forgetting as leaving what has been entrusted and links memory to a later reminder. The psalm's educational purpose is that later generations not forget God's works but keep the commandments, an explicit memory-obedience relation.

column5: a book of remembrance for those who fear God and esteem the name
column6: The commentary connects unforgetting, divine knowledge, and a lasting written record. Malachi describes God attending to those who speak together in reverence and a book of remembrance being written before him, a reciprocal scene of human remembrance and divine record.

column5: Moses receives Torah and transmits it through successive teachers
column6: The commentary emphasizes that a sourced word reaches a recipient and then others. Avot begins its chain with Moses receiving Torah at Sinai and handing it to Joshua, elders, prophets, and the assembly, a rabbinic model of guarded transmission across generations.

column5: repeated teaching from Moses through Israel
column6: The commentary describes the instructor reading first and the recipient following so the word remains. The Talmud's account of Moses teaching Aaron, his sons, elders, and all Israel in repeated cycles makes repetition the concrete practice by which revelation is retained and shared.

column5: twenty-four restored books made public for reading
column6: The commentary sets preserved recitation beside enduring pages and asks how a word reaches later hearers. After Ezra's inspired restoration of books, the Most High orders the first twenty-four made public for worthy and unworthy readers, a Jewish account of recovered revelation opened for communal use.

column5: seventy restored books reserved for the wise
column6: The commentary distinguishes what is openly uttered from what remains hidden under God's control. The next instruction reserves the remaining books for the wise, a Jewish apocalyptic counterpoint in which preservation does not imply unrestricted disclosure.

column5: Jewish refusal to add, remove, or alter sacred books
column6: The commentary claims that the divine source protects the given word from loss and change. Josephus describes a Jewish conviction that no one has dared add to, take from, or alter the ancestral books, a later Jewish articulation of scriptural preservation.

column5: apostolic preaching handed on in written Gospels
column6: The commentary moves from a word received by a messenger to a durable body of pages for later readers. Irenaeus describes the apostles first preaching and then handing down the Gospel in writings, a patristic account of oral revelation becoming preserved Scripture.

column5: Spirit gives utterance to the gathered speakers
column6: The commentary's causative verb makes speech possible through God's action. At Pentecost the gathered disciples begin speaking as the Spirit gives them utterance; the speech is multilingual rather than a recited book, so the link is an enabled-utterance motif.

column5: faith comes through hearing the proclaimed word
column6: The commentary presents recitation as a word carried from its source into the hearer's life. Paul grounds faith in hearing, and hearing in Christ's word, offering a Christian account of oral proclamation as the means by which a message reaches and changes its audience.

column5: public reading, exhortation, and teaching
column6: The commentary treats reading as more than isolated sound: retained words become reminder and instruction. Timothy is charged with public reading, exhortation, and teaching, a church practice that joins recitation to its communal effect.

column5: holding fast the taught word in order to exhort others
column6: The commentary says the recipient must retain the word so that others may be reminded. Titus' overseer holds firmly to the trustworthy word according to teaching in order to exhort and answer opponents, an office-specific parallel to retention becoming instruction.

column5: close attention to what was heard lest it drift away
column6: The commentary's promise removes the danger that the given word will be dropped or forgotten. Hebrews warns hearers to pay closer attention to what they have heard so that they do not drift away, the ordinary human vulnerability against which the Qur'anic assurance stands out.

column5: what was heard from the beginning remaining within
column6: The commentary's gathered word remains in the recipient rather than becoming discarded residue. First John tells believers to let what they heard from the beginning remain in them, making continuance in the received message the condition of continuing communion.
